subject: Art & Design
title: Romanticism: Emotion Over Reason
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Romanticism: Emotion Over Reason.

hook.text: The Enlightenment said reason rules everything. Romantic painters said: not so fast.

buildup.text: Delacroix, Turner, and Friedrich painted storms, ruins, and overwhelming natural landscapes.

discovery.text: The concept of the 'sublime' — beauty mixed with terror — became art's highest goal.

twist.text: Romanticism wasn't anti-science. It argued that feelings are a valid way to understand the world.

climax.text: Caspar David Friedrich's Wanderer Above the Sea of Fog became the movement's iconic image.

punchline.text: Romanticism said: feel first, analyze later.

quiz.question: What was the Romantic movement's core belief about art?
options: Emotion and feeling are valid ways to understand the world

details.summary: Romanticism (late 18th-mid 19th century) rejected Enlightenment rationalism in favor of emotion, nature, and individual expression. Painters like Turner, Friedrich, and Delacroix depicted sublime landscapes, storms, and human passion, celebrating feelings as the highest form of truth.
details.whyItMatters: Romanticism established the modern idea of the artist as an emotional visionary rather than a skilled craftsman. It valorized nature, individual feeling, and imagination — ideals that remain central to how we think about creativity today.
takeaways: Rejected rationalism in favor of emotion and nature
Turner, Friedrich, and Delacroix were leading painters
Established the modern idea of the artist as emotional visionary

faq.question: What is 'the sublime' in Romantic art?
faq.answer: A feeling of awe mixed with terror inspired by nature's overwhelming power — vast mountains, violent storms, infinite oceans. Romantic artists sought to capture this experience, showing humans dwarfed by nature's grandeur to inspire both wonder and humility.

faq.question: How did Romanticism react against the Enlightenment?
faq.answer: The Enlightenment prioritized reason, science, and order. Romantics felt this left out essential human experiences — passion, mystery, spiritual longing, and the irrational. They championed emotion, imagination, and individual subjective experience as equally valid paths to truth.
